summary: OSPFv3 can run multiple protocol instances on one interface. This RFC defines an OSPFv2 Instance ID so separate OSPFv2 instances can run on one interface, which supports multiple routing domains on the same subnet.

eli5.summary: One road, several maps. This labels each map so routers can follow the right one even when many share the same road.

questions: multiple ospf instances on an interface
what is the ospfv2 instance id
how to run multiple ospf instances on one interface
what does rfc 6549 change in the ospf header
subtitle: A one-byte Instance ID in the OSPFv2 packet header lets several OSPF instances share one interface.

tldr.problem: OSPFv2 had no way to tell packets of separate protocol instances apart on the same interface, so multiple routing domains could not share a subnet.
tldr.mechanism: The 16-bit Authentication Type field is split into an 8-bit Instance ID and an 8-bit AuType, and a router discards packets whose Instance ID does not match one of its configured instances on that interface.
tldr.outcome: Several OSPFv2 instances can run on one interface. Routers that do not support the extension drop non-zero-instance packets as an authentication type mismatch, which the RFC says is the desired result.

today: RFC 6549 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2328, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why OSPFv2 Needs Instances
sections.content:
OSPFv3 already has a mechanism for running multiple instances of the protocol on one interface. RFC 6549 brings the same idea to OSPFv2, so that separate routing domains can live on the same subnet.

There is one deliberate difference. In OSPFv3 the Instance ID can be used for several purposes, such as putting the same interface in multiple areas. In OSPFv2 the Instance ID is reserved for identifying protocol instances and nothing else.

The document updates RFC 2328, the base OSPF Version 2 specification.
sections.eli5: Normally one set of routers shares a road and one map. This lets several groups share the same road while each follows its own map.

sections.title: The Modified Packet Header
sections.content:
To tell instances apart, the packet header changes in one place. The old 16-bit Authentication Type field is split into two 8-bit fields: a new Instance ID and the AuType. All other fields keep their meaning from RFC 2328, and AuType keeps its meaning too, just in 8 bits instead of 16.

The Instance ID lets multiple OSPFv2 instances use one interface. Each instance gets its own ID, and the ID has local subnet significance only.

The receive rule is firm: a received packet whose Instance ID is not equal to one of the Instance IDs of the OSPFv2 instances configured on the receiving interface MUST be discarded.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a small number label in a spot that used to be bigger than it needed to be. If the label is not one of yours, you throw the message away.

sections.title: Interface Instance IDs
sections.content:
The conceptual interface data structure from Section 9 of RFC 2328 gains an Interface Instance ID. It defaults to 0, and a non-zero value may be set through configuration.

When sending, the router puts the interface's Instance ID in the packet header. When receiving, it uses the header's Instance ID to demultiplex the packet to the right OSPFv2 instance, and discards packets that match none of the interface's configured instances.

Some values are defined. Instance ID 0 is the Base IPv4 Unicast Instance, which keeps backward compatibility with the base OSPF specification. Values 3 to 127 are private use, left to the local network administrator. The RFC suggests, for example, independent non-congruent topologies for different classes of IPv4 unicast traffic, but leaves the details out of scope.

The first three Instance IDs are analogous to the topology IDs defined in RFC 4915. Sharing state between instances as an optimization is explicitly left for further study.
sections.eli5: Number 0 is the normal map everyone already uses. A few other numbers are set aside for special maps, and a big block is left for each network owner to use however they like.

sections.title: Authentication and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Because AuType shrank from 2 octets to 1, routers that do not support this specification see a non-zero Instance ID as part of the AuType. They treat it as a mismatched authentication type and drop the packet. The RFC says this is exactly what is desired, since such routers should only support the default instance. It is solely due to the field definition, not any change to OSPFv2 authentication.

The document notes an earlier worry that some implementations would log every authentication type mismatch. Discussions with implementers concluded it is not as severe as feared, since most implementations dampen the logging, so the more drastic mechanisms to keep legacy routers from receiving such multicast packets were removed.

If the OSPF MIB from RFC 4750 is implemented, the authentication failure SNMP notifications would be undesirable on mixed subnets. Implementations of both are therefore recommended to support SNMP notification filtering as in Section 6 of RFC 3413.
sections.eli5: An old router does not know about the new number label and thinks the message has a wrong password stamp, so it ignores it. That is just what we want.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The extension adds no security considerations beyond those of OSPFv2, which are described in RFC 2328. The RFC adds that, given only three OSPFv2 authentication types have been standardized, reducing the header field to 8 bits seems reasonable.
sections.eli5: Adding the number label does not make anything less safe than before. Only three kinds of passwords exist, so a smaller box for them is plenty.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
The AuType field shrinks, so values 256 to 65535 in the OSPF Authentication Codes registry are no longer defined and are deprecated. The RFC says this causes no compatibility issue because that range was previously 'Reserved and should not be assigned'.

A new registry for OSPFv2 Instance IDs is created. Value 0 is the Base IPv4 Unicast Instance, 1 the Base IPv4 Multicast Instance, 2 the Base IPv4 In-band Management Instance, and 3 to 127 is Private Use. The range 128 to 255 is Unassigned and needs Standards Action.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers gets a new page for instance labels. Some are taken, some are for anyone's private use, and the rest are saved for later.

fields.name: Instance ID
fields.desc: New field. Selects the OSPFv2 instance on the interface.

fields.name: AuType
fields.desc: Authentication type, reduced from 16 bits to 8.

items.label: Base IPv4 Unicast
items.desc: Default instance; backward compatible with base OSPF.

items.label: Base IPv4 Multicast
items.desc: Separate routing table used for RPF checking of IPv4 multicast traffic.

items.label: Base IPv4 In-band Management
items.desc: Separate routing table for network management applications.

items.label: Private Use
items.desc: Defined by the local network administrator.
